results.content: **You are here** Research > Retention. For any research project which uses personal data, the motto “*as long as necessary, as short as possible,*” is important. The Principal Investigator should periodically review their research data set/s to assess whether personal data is still required. When planning and designing a research project, the Principal Investigator should establish at what stage personal data will be: pseudonymised (de-identified), archived, anonymised. This ensures that the retention period for personal data is appropriate to the requirements of the research project. In line with the principle of transparency, the retention period **or the criteria used to calculate that retention period** should be shared with the research participant in your project specific Information Leaflet. ## Determining the retention period for research projects using personal data. Research data should be retained in a secure manner by the University for as long as it is of continuing use to the University. If the research data may be of value to the University (in terms of secondary analysis), consider this at the outset, so that participants are informed at the time of data collection of any possible future use of their data. Individuals’ rights in relation to the retention of their personal data may override the retention periods indicated above. If any request is received from a research participant to remove their personal data from a research project, contact the College Research DPO for advice without delay at researchdpo@tcd.ie. They should only be stored for as long as you are processing the participant’s personal data for research purposes (to evidence the ethical principle of informed consent, or compliance with the Health Research Regulations, if health research). This advice is subject to of any other retention requirements regarding consent which may be imposed by the funder, publisher, law, regulation or best practice in your particular area of research. If you are unclear about how long you should retain personal data, the College Research DPO can be contacted for advice, at researchDPO@tcd.ie. results.title: GDPR Data Retention: How Long Should You Keep Data?
results.content: CookieYes - Cookie Consent Management Platform. # GDPR Data Retention: How Long Should You Keep Data? This article offers a detailed guide on GDPR data retention, covering best practices, criteria for determining retention periods, and how CookieYes can simplify compliance through effective tools and technologies. Data retention is the practice of storing personal data for a specific period to meet legal, regulatory, or business needs. Retention policies define how long data is stored and when it should be deleted or anonymised to comply with privacy laws and protect individuals’ rights. GDPR emphasises the “storage limitation” principle in Article 5, which mandates that personal data must not be kept longer than necessary for the purposes for which it was processed. gdpr how long keep data data retention article 5. While the GDPR does not specify exact retention periods, it requires data controllers to establish retention periods based on the specific purpose of data processing.

results.title: Data Retention Periods: Finding the Right Balance
results.content: However, there is a fine line between retaining data for long enough to derive value from it and holding on to it for too long, potentially infringing on privacy rights and increasing security risks. It is crucial to strike a balance between retaining data for as long as it is necessary for legitimate business purposes and respecting data subject rights. When it comes to the retention of personal data, organizations must consider various factors to determine the appropriate retention period. On the other hand, personal data collected for legal, financial, or archival purposes may require longer retention periods to comply with legal obligations or protect the rights and interests of the organization and its stakeholders. It is important for organizations to conduct a thorough analysis of the data they collect and process. These factors can include the nature of the data, its sensitivity, the purposes for which it is processed, the potential risks associated with its retention, and any applicable legal or regulatory requirements.

results.content:
Title: Ensuring Ethical Tech Use in Data Analysis and Security | Viable Insights
# Ensuring Ethical Tech Use in Data Analysis and Security. IRBs are tasked with ensuring that research involving human subjects is conducted ethically, safeguarding the rights and welfare of participants. Throughout this blog, we’ll explore the intersection of IRBs, technology in data analysis, and data security, shedding light on their importance and best practices for compliance. IRBs are committees established to review and approve research involving human subjects, ensuring that ethical standards are upheld. They evaluate research proposals to ensure that the methods and procedures protect participants from harm and respect their rights. Technological advancements in data analysis, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, have transformed the research landscape. 1. **Informed Consent**: When using advanced data analysis techniques, ensuring that participants fully understand how their data will be used can be challenging. IRBs must ensure that researchers implement measures to detect and mitigate biases to avoid unfair treatment of any group. ### **Data Security: Protecting Participant Information**. Data security is paramount in research involving human subjects, particularly when dealing with sensitive information. IRBs require researchers to implement robust data security measures to protect participant data from unauthorized access, breaches, and other security threats. IRBs assess the encryption standards used and ensure they meet current best practices. IRBs may require researchers to have procedures in place for continuous assessment of data security practices. To ensure compliance with IRB requirements and uphold ethical standards in research, researchers should adhere to the following best practices:. 3. **Implement Strong Data Security Measures**: Adopt industry-standard data security practices, including encryption, access controls, and regular audits. 4. **Stay Informed About Regulatory Changes**: Data protection regulations and ethical standards are continuously evolving. Researchers should stay informed about changes in regulations and best practices to ensure ongoing compliance. As technology continues to advance, the role of IRBs in ensuring ethical research practices becomes increasingly important. By carefully reviewing research proposals, assessing data security measures, and promoting ethical standards, IRBs help protect the rights and welfare of research participants. Researchers, in turn, must engage with IRBs proactively, implement robust data security measures, and adhere to best practices to ensure their research is both innovative and ethical.

results.content:
Title: Ethical issues in clinical research and publication
Review article Ethical issues in clinical research and publication. * :   Clinical research including human participants should be based on truth, demonstrate scientific integrity, and follow ethical standards and guidelines to protect study participants. In this article, basic ethical issues in clinical research and publication are reviewed and summarized based on recent guidelines. * **Keywords**: Clinical study; Publications; Research ethic. Clinical research should be based on ethical standards that respect the research participants and protect their health and rights. This is a review of ethical issues in clinical research and publication that must be considered by any researcher who conducts research on humans. Despite this, several reports of unethical medical studies conducted without informed consent on vulnerable research participants have been published since the early 1960s [4,5]. Among several declarations related to research ethics [7-9], the Declaration of Helsinki published by the World Medical Association in 1964 has undergone revision and is now accepted as an ethical principle in medical research involving humans [10-12]. In case there is no legally authorized representative and the research cannot be delayed, the research may proceed without informed consent provided the reason for not obtaining consent is included in the research protocol with approval of the research ethics committee. The submitted manuscript should state that the study was approved by the research ethics committee or institutional review board, and that it was undertaken with informed consent from the research participants [1,6]. The ICMJE has pledged not to review or publish studies based on contracts that restrict independent access to and analysis of research data and free publication of research results [27]. :   Every medical or clinical study that includes human participants should be designed and conducted to achieve scientific integrity as well as to follow ethical principles to protect the health, safety, and well-being of the participants.
